title: Estimating Populations You Cannot All See
endLine: Mark and revisit to estimate populations and separate misses from loss.

scenes.tts: How do you count animals when most stay hidden? One visit misses them, and a missing animal may not be dead. Mark-recapture uses repeated sightings to estimate abundance, survival and occupancy.
scenes.caption: How do you count animals when most stay hidden? One visit misses them, and a missing animal may not be dead. Mark-recapture uses repeated sightings to estimate abundance, survival and occupancy.
scenes.visual: Top-down view of a sunlit wetland pond with reed patches (schematic): dozens of small fish-like silhouettes drift in and out of cover so only a fraction are visible at once, while a large question mark hovers over the reeds; one marked silhouette slips behind reeds and two icons pulse beside it, an X and an outward arrow, then fade into three clean readouts: Abundance, Survival, Occupancy.
scenes.narration: How do you count animals when most stay hidden? One visit misses them, and a missing animal may not be dead. Mark-recapture uses repeated sightings to estimate abundance, survival and occupancy.

scenes.tts: Start in a closed pond, with no births, deaths, or animals leaving. Catch and mark fifty animals, then release them to mix in. Later, catch ninety and count the overlap: twenty already carry your mark.
scenes.caption: Start in a closed pond, with no births, deaths, or animals leaving. Catch and mark 50 animals, then release them to mix in. Later, catch 90 and count the overlap: 20 already carry your mark.
scenes.visual: Same pond world, now ringed by a crisp closed boundary labelled 'Closed pond' (schematic). A net sweeps in, highlights 50 silhouettes with bright gold marks (counter shows n1 = 50), and releases them to drift evenly among unmarked silhouettes. A second sweep gathers 90 silhouettes into a holding ring (n2 = 90), and the 20 gold-marked ones glow together as the overlap (m2 = 20).
scenes.narration: Start in a closed pond, with no births, deaths, or animals leaving. Catch and mark 50 animals, then release them to mix in. Later, catch 90 and count the overlap: 20 already carry your mark.

scenes.tts: The marked share of the second catch estimates the marked share of the whole pond. Multiply first catch by second, then divide by marked recaptures: the Lincoln-Petersen formula. Fifty times ninety is four thousand five hundred; divided by twenty gives two hundred twenty-five.
scenes.caption: The marked share of the second catch estimates the marked share of the whole pond. Multiply first catch by second, then divide by marked recaptures: the Lincoln-Petersen formula. 50 × 90 is 4,500; divided by 20 gives 225.
scenes.visual: Beside the pond, two proportion bars align (computed from given numbers): 20/90 next to 50/N, rearranging into N = n1 × n2 / m2. As each number is spoken, 50 × 90 = 4,500 appears, then 4,500 / 20 = 225, and the pond gently reveals its estimated 225 silhouettes (schematic).
scenes.narration: The marked share of the second catch estimates the marked share of the whole pond. Multiply first catch by second, then divide by marked recaptures: the Lincoln-Petersen formula. 50 × 90 is 4,500; divided by 20 gives 225.

scenes.tts: The plain estimate runs high with small samples. Chapman's version adds one to each count: fifty-one times ninety-one, over twenty-one, minus one gives two hundred twenty.
scenes.caption: The plain estimate runs high with small samples. Chapman's version adds 1 to each count: (51 × 91) / 21 − 1 gives 220.
scenes.visual: The 225 estimate sits in the corner as each count increments by 1 beside the pond, and the computed Chapman line writes itself as it is spoken: (51 × 91) / 21 − 1 = 4,641 / 21 − 1 = 220. The two estimates, 225 and 220, stand side by side (schematic).
scenes.narration: The plain estimate runs high with small samples. Chapman's version adds 1 to each count: (51 × 91) / 21 − 1 gives 220.

scenes.tts: That proportion works only if marks stay readable and every animal is equally catchable. Suppose marked animals learn to avoid traps and enter the second catch less often. Will the estimate come out too high or too low?
scenes.caption: That proportion works only if marks stay readable and every animal is equally catchable. Suppose marked animals learn to avoid traps and enter the second catch less often. Will the estimate come out too high or too low?
scenes.visual: In the same pond (schematic), a trap lowers into the water while gold-marked silhouettes veer away from its opening as unmarked silhouettes drift in. Above the pond, a high-contrast question card appears: 'Trap-shy marked animals: estimate too high or too low?'
scenes.narration: That proportion works only if marks stay readable and every animal is equally catchable. Suppose marked animals learn to avoid traps and enter the second catch less often. Will the estimate come out too high or too low?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the question card 'Trap-shy marked animals: estimate too high or too low?' stays on screen while marked silhouettes slowly steer around the trap in gentle ambient motion and the formula N = n1 × n2 / m2 pulses subtly on m2 (schematic).

scenes.tts: Too high: trap-shy marked animals shrink the overlap, so you divide by too little. Trap-happy animals do the reverse and shrink the estimate. Photo identification avoids handling, as in a 2018 Quito dog survey, but can mismatch individuals. Every result is an estimate, not a head count.
scenes.caption: Too high: trap-shy marked animals shrink the overlap, so you divide by too little. Trap-happy animals do the reverse and shrink the estimate. Photo identification avoids handling, as in a 2018 Quito dog survey, but can mismatch individuals. Every result is an estimate, not a head count.
scenes.visual: The denominator m2 in N = n1 × n2 / m2 shrinks as gold-marked silhouettes stay outside the trap, pushing the N gauge upward (schematic); then marked silhouettes crowd into the trap, enlarging m2 and pulling N downward. A camera shutter icon replaces the trap with two dog-pattern photo cards (schematic, 'Quito, 2018') showing a brief mismatch flash, then a clean banner: 'Estimate, not head count'.
scenes.narration: Too high: trap-shy marked animals shrink the overlap, so you divide by too little. Trap-happy animals do the reverse and shrink the estimate. Photo identification avoids handling, as in a 2018 Quito dog survey, but can mismatch individuals. Every result is an estimate, not a head count.

scenes.tts: Over longer intervals, populations open: animals die or move. On repeated visits, an animal seen after a gap was alive and missed, separating detection from survival. Still, a survivor that leaves looks dead. Apparent survival is true survival times site fidelity: the chance a survivor stays in the area. Searching nearby sites and double-marking catch emigration and mark loss.
scenes.caption: Over longer intervals, populations open: animals die or move. On repeated visits, an animal seen after a gap was alive and missed, separating detection from survival. Still, a survivor that leaves looks dead. Apparent survival is true survival times site fidelity: the chance a survivor stays in the area. Searching nearby sites and double-marking catch emigration and mark loss.
scenes.visual: The pond boundary opens into a connected landscape with a neighbouring pond (schematic). A timeline of repeated visits builds an encounter history '1 0 1' for one marked animal: the middle '0' glows 'Alive and missed'. After the last '1', a dashed arrow carries the animal into the neighbouring pond while the equation 'Apparent survival = true survival × site fidelity (chance of staying)' appears. A search ring expands to the neighbouring pond and a second coloured mark snaps onto an animal to show double-marking.
scenes.narration: Over longer intervals, populations open: animals die or move. On repeated visits, an animal seen after a gap was alive and missed, separating detection from survival. Still, a survivor that leaves looks dead. Apparent survival is true survival times site fidelity: the chance a survivor stays in the area. Searching nearby sites and double-marking catch emigration and mark loss.

scenes.tts: Marking and revisiting unlocked findings single counts miss. On the Galapagos island Daphne Major, Boag and Grant banded and measured nearly every medium ground finch. After the 1977 drought killed roughly eighty-five percent, their 1981 report showed larger birds survived best. Males with larger beaks did best. Beak and body size go together, so the target trait is unclear.
scenes.caption: Marking and revisiting unlocked findings single counts miss. On the Galapagos island Daphne Major, Boag and Grant banded and measured nearly every medium ground finch. After the 1977 drought killed roughly 85 percent, their 1981 report showed larger birds survived best. Males with larger beaks did best. Beak and body size go together, so the target trait is unclear.
scenes.visual: Field card emerging from the landscape world labelled 'Daphne Major, Galapagos, 1977-1981' (schematic): banded finch silhouettes with coloured leg bands stand on dry volcanic ground; a survival bar drops by roughly 85 percent while larger silhouettes with deeper beaks remain highlighted at the top, with a tag reading 'beak and body size correlated'.
scenes.narration: Marking and revisiting unlocked findings single counts miss. On the Galapagos island Daphne Major, Boag and Grant banded and measured nearly every medium ground finch. Beak and body size go together, so the target trait is unclear.

scenes.tts: In 2006, Olendorf and colleagues recaptured marked male guppies in three Trinidad streams. They set morphs at about three common to one rare, reversing which pattern was rare. After fifteen or seventeen days, rare males had higher estimated survival, if missing fish died rather than moved.
scenes.caption: In 2006, Olendorf and colleagues recaptured marked male guppies in three Trinidad streams. They set morphs at about 3 common to 1 rare, reversing which pattern was rare. After 15 or 17 days, rare males had higher estimated survival, if missing fish died rather than moved.
scenes.visual: Field card labelled 'Trinidad streams, 2006' showing two side-by-side stream pools (schematic): left pool holds 3 plain to 1 spotted male guppy, right pool reverses to 3 spotted to 1 plain, with the rare morph ringed in gold. After a '15–17 days' sweep, the rare morph in each pool stays highlighted with higher recapture survival, beside a small assumption tag: 'Missing = died, not moved'.
scenes.narration: In 2006, Olendorf and colleagues recaptured marked male guppies in three Trinidad streams. They set morphs at about 3 common to 1 rare, reversing which pattern was rare. After 15 or 17 days, rare males had higher estimated survival, if missing fish died rather than moved.

scenes.tts: Zeros are ambiguous: absent, or just missed. In 2002, MacKenzie and colleagues analysed repeat Maryland wetland surveys from 2000. American toads were detected at ten of twenty-nine wetlands, about zero point three four. Modelling detection raised occupancy to zero point four nine. Repeated marks and visits separate missed animals from true loss.
scenes.caption: Zeros are ambiguous: absent, or just missed. In 2002, MacKenzie and colleagues analysed repeat Maryland wetland surveys from 2000. American toads were detected at 10 of 29 wetlands, about 0.34. Modelling detection raised occupancy to 0.49. Repeated marks and visits separate missed animals from true loss.
scenes.visual: Grid of 29 small wetland ponds (schematic, 'Maryland, 2000; MacKenzie et al., 2002'): 10 light up as detected while the rest show '000' histories. A computed bar chart rises from 'Detected: 0.34' (10/29) to 'Estimated occupancy: 0.49' as several hidden toad silhouettes glow softly inside '000' ponds. All ponds pulse gently together to echo the opening pond world.
scenes.narration: Zeros are ambiguous: absent, or just missed. In 2002, MacKenzie and colleagues analysed repeat Maryland wetland surveys from 2000. American toads were detected at 10 of 29 wetlands, about 0.34. Modelling detection raised occupancy to 0.49. Repeated marks and visits separate missed animals from true loss.

scenes.visual: Silent end card on a clean dark frame with subtle drifting water-ripple motion (schematic), displaying in large high-contrast text: 'Mark and revisit to estimate populations and separate misses from loss.'
